title: IB Global Politics Common Mistakes and Fixes
summary: IB Global Politics common mistakes cost easy marks. Learn to read command terms, use precise evidence, manage timing, and answer confidently under pressure.
body_markdown:
The frustrating thing about an IB Global Politics exam is that knowledge alone does not protect your marks. You can understand sovereignty, legitimacy, human rights and development, yet still underperform because you evaluated when the question asked you to compare, presented evidence without analysing it, or spent too long perfecting an early response.


The most common mistakes are surprisingly practical: misreading command terms, failing to answer every part of the question, using vague evidence, losing sight of the required unit of analysis, and managing time emotionally rather than strategically. Each has a fix. The key is to practise the act of answering, not simply the act of remembering.


### A quick exam mistake checklist


Before submitting an answer, ask:


- Have I followed the command term?
- Have I answered every part of the question?
- Is my evidence specific enough to verify the claim?
- Have I identified the relevant actor, place, period or level of analysis?
- Have I explained how each example supports my argument?
- Have I considered another perspective or limitation where appropriate?
- Have I left enough time to complete every required response?
- Does my conclusion make a defensible judgment?


These checks sound simple. Under pressure, simple things are often the first things to disappear.


### The student who knew too much and answered too little


Imagine a student called Maya. She is hypothetical, but her exam experience will feel familiar to many Global Politics students.


Maya enters the exam with detailed knowledge of humanitarian intervention, climate negotiations, structural violence and the influence of non-state actors. She has memorised cases from several regions. When she sees a familiar topic, she starts writing immediately.


Her first paragraph is informed and fluent. Unfortunately, the question asks her to evaluate a claim, while most of her response explains the topic. She refers to the United Nations but does not name a resolution, institution, decision or date. She spends too long adding context, rushes the final section and finishes with a conclusion that merely repeats her introduction.


Nothing went dramatically wrong. That is precisely the problem. Maya lost accessible marks through several small decisions.


A student brings an enormous suitcase of knowledge to answer one small exam question


### Mistake: misreading the command term


Command terms define the intellectual task. A response can contain accurate political knowledge and still be poorly matched to the question.


For example:


- **Identify** requires a concise, accurate selection.
- **Explain** requires reasons, mechanisms or causal links.
- **Compare** requires sustained attention to similarities between two or more items.
- **Contrast** focuses on differences.
- **Analyse** requires you to break an issue into relevant relationships, causes or implications.
- **Discuss** expects a balanced review supported by evidence.
- **Evaluate** requires a judgment about strengths, limitations, significance or validity.
- **To what extent** requires a qualified conclusion about how far a claim holds.


One recurring lesson associated with IB Global Politics examiner reports is that candidates should answer the question actually set, rather than reproducing a prepared essay on the same broad topic. A useful defence is to underline the command term, circle the political issue and identify the scope before planning.


The[IB Global Politics Paper 1 answering guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-answer-ib-global-politics-paper-1-questions) explains how command terms shape source-based responses. For extended writing, use the[Paper 2 essay structure guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-structure-ib-global-politics-paper-2-essays) to turn the command term into a clear thesis.


### The fix: translate the task


Before writing, complete this sentence mentally:


> To answer this question, I must...


For an evaluate question, the ending might be: assess the claim using strengths, limitations and a supported judgment. For a compare question, it might be: examine similarities throughout the response, using both cases directly.


This translation takes seconds and can prevent an entire answer from drifting off task.


### Mistake: naming evidence without using it


Global Politics rewards relevant political analysis, not a catalogue of events. A country name is not automatically evidence. Neither is a passing reference to a conflict, protest movement or international institution.


Weak evidence often sounds like this: “The United Nations has tried to protect human rights in many conflicts.” The statement may be broadly defensible, but it is too general to carry much analytical weight.


Stronger evidence identifies what happened, who acted, where and why it matters. It then connects those details to the argument. The useful sequence is:


**Claim, evidence, explanation, qualification.**


Your explanation is the bridge. Without it, the examiner has to infer why the example supports your answer. That is work your response should do explicitly.


Students who need a repeatable paragraph method can use the[guide to writing a strong Global Politics essay](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-write-a-top-scoring-ib-global-politics-essay-or-expert-revisiondojo-techniques) . The[Global Politics essay mistakes guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/common-mistakes-in-ib-global-politics-essays) also helps distinguish description from analysis.


### The fix: build evidence cards with a purpose


Do not revise case studies as long narratives. Build compact evidence cards containing:


- actor or institution
- event, policy or decision
- approximate date or period
- relevant political concept
- argument the evidence supports
- limitation or alternative interpretation


This makes evidence adaptable. One case may illuminate power, legitimacy and interdependence differently, depending on the question.


### Mistake: omitting the requested unit or scope


Global Politics rarely depends on numerical units, but it constantly depends on units of analysis. Is the question about individuals, states, international organisations, non-state actors or the global system? Is it asking about one specified case, multiple sources, a defined period or a particular political concept?


A student may discuss climate governance while ignoring that the question specifically concerns non-state actors. Another may evaluate state sovereignty without distinguishing domestic authority from external recognition. If numerical evidence is used, its unit and timeframe also need to be clear. A percentage without a population, place or year can mislead more than it informs.


### The fix: mark the boundaries


Beside the question, note three things:


- **Task:** What must I do?
- **Subject:** What political issue or concept must I address?
- **Boundary:** Which actors, sources, places or periods must remain central?


Return to these boundaries after each paragraph. A sophisticated point outside the question earns less than a focused point inside it.


### Mistake: treating sources as decoration


In source-based work, students sometimes paraphrase a source and move on. Others inject extensive own knowledge without using the material provided. Both approaches miss the relationship between source interpretation and political understanding.


When referring to a source, identify its actual claim or implication. Then connect it to the question. If evaluation is required, consider perspective, purpose, context or what the source cannot establish. Avoid generic statements such as “the source may be biased” unless you explain the relevant limitation.


Use the[RevisionDojo Global Politics Paper 2 guide notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-global-politics/ib-global-politics-paper-2-guide/notes) alongside source-response practice to keep command-term expectations visible.


### Mistake: allowing one answer to consume the exam


Timing problems often begin with good intentions. A student wants the first answer to be excellent, so they keep adding detail. The remaining questions then become shorter, less analytical and sometimes incomplete.


An unfinished answer creates a difficult trade-off. The extra sentence added earlier may be less valuable than the entire paragraph that was never attempted later.


### The fix: budget time before writing


Use the duration and mark allocation shown on your current examination paper and course materials. Reserve time to read and plan, divide the main writing period proportionally, and protect a short final check. Set hard stopping points for each response.


Timed practice is essential because timing is not merely organisational. It affects judgment. You need to learn when another example improves an answer and when it simply delays the next one.


The[guide to revising IB Global Politics effectively](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-revise-effectively-for-ib-global-politics) combines concept review with active recall and timed writing. When you are ready, open the[IB Global Politics Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-global-politics/questionbank) , select a focused set of questions and then sit timed papers in Exam Mode.


### A better way to review practice answers


Do not finish a response, read it once and label it “good” or “bad.” Diagnose the failure precisely.


Classify each lost opportunity as one of the following:


- command-term error
- incomplete response
- vague evidence
- missing explanation
- weak counterargument
- unsupported judgment
- source misuse
- timing problem


Then rewrite only the weakest section. This is more efficient than repeatedly producing full essays without changing the underlying habit.

### Turn easy marks into dependable marks


Maya’s hypothetical problem was not a lack of intelligence or effort. She had knowledge, but the exam asked her to control it. That distinction matters.


The most reliable improvement comes from making small exam behaviours automatic: translate the command term, define the scope, choose precise evidence, explain its relevance and stop when the time budget says stop.


Knowledge gives you material. Technique makes that material count. Practise both in the RevisionDojo Questionbank, then sit timed papers in Exam Mode until focused decision-making feels ordinary, even when the clock does not.
